analogy.p: Think of the rainforest nutrient cycle as a shopping centre where goods are sold the moment they are delivered. The shops (the **biomass**) hold nearly all the stock, the warehouse (the **soil**) is almost empty because deliveries go straight to the shelves, and rubbish (the **litter**) is cleared away within hours. This maps well to the fast recycling of nutrients and thin, infertile soil. It breaks down because a shopping centre gets deliveries from outside every day, whereas the rainforest relies mostly on recycling its own nutrients, with only small inputs from rain and rock weathering.
analogy.t: The rainforest as a busy shopping centre with no storage room

bullets: **Location**: found close to the **equator**, roughly between 10°N and 10°S (the tropics), mainly in South America (Amazon basin), central Africa (Congo basin) and south-east Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia).
**Climate**: hot and wet all year, with little seasonal change in temperature and heavy rainfall every month.
**Structure**: vertical layers (emergent, canopy, understorey, shrub layer and forest floor) each with different light levels and different species.
**Adaptations**: plants and animals have specific features that help them survive heat, wetness, shade and competition.
**Interdependence**: nutrients cycle quickly between biomass, litter and soil; remove one part and the rest suffers.
**Biodiversity**: tropical rainforests contain more species than any other terrestrial biome.
Command words you will meet: **describe**, **explain**, **suggest**, and 4, 6 or 9 mark **assess** questions that need a case study.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 (The living world) expects you to describe the **characteristics of tropical rainforests**: where they are, their climate, their structure, their soils and their huge biodiversity. You must also explain **how plants and animals have adapted** to the conditions and show how the rainforest is an **interdependent system** in which climate, soil, water, plants, animals and people are linked. These ideas feed straight into later points on deforestation and sustainable management, so this is the foundation topic for the whole rainforest strand.

bullets: The **Amazon basin** (Brazil, Peru, Colombia and neighbouring countries) is the largest rainforest, with the Amazon River draining it.
The **Congo basin** in central Africa is the second largest; **Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea** hold the main south-east Asian rainforests.
High sun angle means intense insolation; this heats the ground, and **warm air rises** at the equator (low pressure belt, the ITCZ).
Rising air cools, water vapour **condenses** and falls as heavy convectional rain, often in the afternoon.
No true winter means plants can grow **all year**, so there is no period when growth stops.
Rainforests also depend on a **supply of water from the ocean and from the forest itself** (transpiration recycles a large share of rainfall).
Exam tip: mention **latitude, sun angle and rising air** when asked why rainforests are near the equator.
core.h: Where are tropical rainforests found and why there?
core.p: Tropical rainforests lie in a belt around the equator, roughly **10° north to 10° south**, with some extensions along warm, wet coasts. The reason is the **global atmospheric circulation**: at the equator the sun's rays strike the surface almost vertically (high angle of incidence), so the energy is concentrated on a small area and the surface is heated strongly. Warm air rises, cools and condenses to form towering cloud and daily convectional rainfall, which is why the equatorial belt is both hot and very wet. Together with the lack of a cold season, this allows continuous plant growth.

bullets: **Temperature**: high (around 27 °C) and almost constant; the **diurnal range** (day to night) is bigger than the annual range.
**Rainfall**: more than about 2000 mm per year; many places have a daily afternoon downpour from convectional storms.
**Humidity**: very high, often above 80 percent; the air feels heavy and damp.
**Seasons**: little change; some regions have a slightly drier period but never a true dry season.

**Reading a climate graph**: temperature is a **line** (right axis in degrees C), rainfall is **bars** (left axis in mm); quote figures with units and use a range, e.g. 'temperature stays between 26 and 28 °C'.
**Why plants grow quickly**: constant warmth, constant moisture and strong sunlight give a long growing season of 12 months.
**Link**: warm, wet conditions also speed decomposition, which matters for the nutrient cycle.
core.p: The climate is **equatorial**: the average temperature is about **26 to 28 °C** in every month, so the annual temperature range is tiny, usually only 1 to 3 °C. Rainfall is typically **over 2000 mm a year** (often more than 2500 mm in the wettest areas) and falls in every month, though some months are slightly drier. Humidity is very high because so much water evaporates from the ground and is transpired by leaves. Day length stays close to 12 hours all year, so there are no seasons in the way the UK has them. A climate graph therefore shows a nearly flat temperature line and a bar for rainfall in every month.

bullets: **Emergent layer**: tallest trees (e.g. kapok, Brazil nut), widely spaced, with umbrella-shaped crowns; exposed to sun and wind.
**Canopy**: thick, continuous leaf layer; about 80 percent of the sunlight is absorbed here; home to monkeys, birds, insects and epiphytes.
**Understorey**: young trees and palms in deep shade, with larger leaves to catch scarce light.
**Shrub layer**: seedlings and shade-tolerant plants; very little light reaches here.
**Forest floor**: often only about 2 percent of sunlight arrives; covered in leaf litter that decomposes fast; fungi and decomposers are abundant.
**Gaps** formed by fallen trees let in light and allow rapid regrowth of seedlings.
Lianas (woody vines) link the layers, and epiphytes live on branches in the canopy.
core.h: Structure of the rainforest: five layers
core.p: The rainforest has a **vertical structure** with layers, each adapted to a different amount of light. At the top the **emergent layer** has the tallest trees (up to about 45 m or more), which stick out above the canopy and receive full sunlight and strong wind. Below it the dense **canopy** (about 30 to 40 m) forms a continuous roof of leaves that intercepts most of the sunlight and rainfall and holds the majority of the animal life. Little light penetrates beneath it, so the **understorey** is dim and the **shrub layer** and **forest floor** are dark and full of young trees waiting for a gap.

bullets: **Biomass** is the largest store because the huge amount of vegetation holds most nutrients.
**Litter** is a small store because decomposition is rapid in the heat and moisture.
**Soil** is the smallest store: nutrients are leached by heavy rain or taken up quickly by roots.
Thick arrows: **litter fall** (biomass to litter), **decomposition** (litter to soil) and **uptake** (soil to biomass).
Thin arrows: **inputs from rainfall and weathering** of rock, and **losses by runoff and leaching**.
The **shallow roots** (and mycorrhizal fungi) capture nutrients before they are washed away.
If the trees are cut down, the biomass store disappears and nutrients are quickly lost: the system is **fragile**.
Exam link: this is why cleared rainforest land farms poorly after 2 to 3 years.
core.h: Soils and the nutrient cycle (Gersmehl model)
core.p: The nutrient cycle in a rainforest is **fast and mostly closed**. Nutrients are held mainly in the **biomass store** (the living plants), a smaller amount in the **litter store** (fallen leaves and dead matter on the surface) and the smallest in the **soil store**. Because it is hot and wet, litter is broken down by decomposers (fungi, bacteria, insects) within weeks, so nutrients are released and then **taken up by roots almost immediately**. Heavy rain washes soluble nutrients out of the soil (leaching), so the soil is **thin and infertile** despite the lush vegetation. In a Gersmehl diagram the circle sizes show the size of each store and the arrows show transfers: thick arrows are large flows.

bullets: Plants depend on **light, heat and water** from the climate and on **nutrients** from the soil and litter.
Animals depend on plants for **food and habitat**; plants depend on animals for **pollination and seed dispersal**.
**Decomposers** keep the nutrient cycle running; without them nutrients would stay locked in dead material.
**Trees intercept rainfall**, reducing the force of rain on the soil, and their roots hold the soil together.
**Transpiration and evaporation** return water vapour to the atmosphere, forming new clouds and rain.
Indigenous peoples such as those of the Amazon use the forest sustainably for food, materials and medicine.
Interdependence means a change to one part (for example removing trees) causes **knock-on effects** through the whole ecosystem.
Good exam answers use linking words: 'this leads to', 'which means', 'as a result'.
core.h: Interdependence of climate, water, soil, plants, animals and people
core.p: A rainforest is a **system** in which every component depends on the others. The climate (warmth and rain) allows dense plant growth; the plants shelter and feed animals; animals pollinate flowers and disperse seeds; decomposers recycle nutrients to the soil; and the soil supports the plants. The forest also controls the climate: a large share of the rainfall comes from water that trees take up and release to the air by **transpiration**, so the forest helps to create its own rain. People who live in the forest, such as indigenous groups, depend on it for food, medicines and shelter and manage it in traditional ways.

bullets: **Drip tips** and waxy leaves: let heavy rain run off quickly, which stops fungi and bacteria growing on wet leaves and prevents damage.
**Buttress roots**: large, wide roots at the base of tall trees that **support** the tree because soils are thin and roots shallow, and also help to take in nutrients over a large area.
**Thin smooth bark**: no need to protect against cold, and it lets rain run off.
**Epiphytes** (e.g. bromeliads, orchids): grow on branches high up to reach light, take water and nutrients from the air and rain, not the soil.
**Lianas**: climb trees using them as support so they reach the canopy light without building thick stems.
**Large leaves** in the understorey: capture as much of the scarce light as possible.
**Tall trees with umbrella crowns**: emergent trees race upwards to reach the light.
**Fast germination and growth** in gaps: seedlings wait in shade then grow quickly when light appears.
core.p: Plants in the rainforest compete fiercely for **light**, and they must cope with constant heavy rain and poor soils. Their adaptations are specific features with a purpose: you must always say **what the feature is, and how it helps**. Many leaves are large and glossy with pointed tips so water runs off quickly, trees grow tall to reach light, and roots spread widely and shallowly to catch nutrients near the surface. Some plants avoid the problem by growing on other plants instead of in the soil.

bullets: **Camouflage**: e.g. green tree frogs, stick insects and moths blend with leaves and bark, so predators cannot see them.
**Warning colours**: bright poison dart frogs advertise that they are toxic, which deters predators.
**Sloths**: move slowly, conserving energy on a low-energy leaf diet; their fur grows algae that provides extra camouflage.
**Prehensile tails and gripping limbs** (monkeys, tree frogs' sticky pads) allow safe movement among branches.
**Large eyes and good hearing** (e.g. nocturnal animals) help them find food and avoid predators in dim light.
**Specialised beaks** (toucans) allow fruit feeding at the end of thin branches.
**Gliding** animals such as flying squirrels and lizards move between trees without descending.
Different species feed in different layers, reducing **competition**.
core.p: Animals in the rainforest have adapted to life in trees, to the dim light and to the fact that food is spread through all layers. Most species live in the canopy, where food (fruit, leaves, nectar, insects) is plentiful. Features such as **camouflage**, **grip** and **specialised diets** help them to avoid predators, move among branches and avoid competing with other species. Many animals are active at night (nocturnal) or feed at different heights, which lets lots of different species share the same space (reduced competition).

bullets: **Biodiversity** = the variety of living organisms in an area (genetic, species and habitat variety).
**Climate regulation**: trees take in carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and store carbon in their biomass, so the forest is a major **carbon store** (a carbon sink).
**Oxygen** is released during photosynthesis (the forest is sometimes called the lungs of the planet, though much of the oxygen is also used by the forest).
**Medicines**: a high proportion of medicines used in modern medicine come from, or are modelled on, rainforest plants.
**Resources**: timber (mahogany), Brazil nuts, rubber, coffee, cocoa, fruits.
**Water cycle**: rainforests regulate rainfall and river flow.
**Indigenous people** depend on the forest for their way of life.
Loss of species is irreversible: extinction removes genetic information for ever.
core.p: Tropical rainforests are the most **biodiverse** terrestrial ecosystem: they cover only a small percentage of the Earth's land but contain around half of the world's plant and animal species by common estimates, and many species have not yet been named. High biodiversity comes from the stable, warm, wet conditions that allow many specialised niches to exist. Rainforests also provide global services: they store huge amounts of carbon, release oxygen through photosynthesis, influence rainfall patterns and supply timber, food, medicines and rubber.

bullets: **Climate graph**: say 'temperature is high all year, between about 26 and 28 °C' and 'rainfall exceeds about 150 mm in most months'.
Quote **highest and lowest** values and calculate the **range** (highest minus lowest) when asked.
Mention **pattern** (little seasonal change) and then **explain** (near the equator, high sun angle).
For Gersmehl diagrams: **biomass > litter > soil** in size; thick arrows mark the quickest transfers.
For layer diagrams: relate **light** to leaf size, plant height and where animals live.
Check the **units** (mm, °C, m) and the **scale** before writing.
Use **specific** names (kapok, buttress roots, epiphytes) rather than 'special features'.
core.h: Interpreting data and diagrams in exams
core.p: Questions on this topic are often based on a **climate graph**, a **food web**, a **cross-section of layers** or a **nutrient cycle diagram**. You earn marks by using the data accurately and linking it to ideas. For a climate graph, always quote figures with units, refer to both temperature and rainfall, and comment on seasonality. For a nutrient cycle, name the stores and the relative size of each and explain why they are that size. For a layers diagram, link each layer's light level to the plants and animals found there.

bullets: **Climate change**: forests are carbon sinks; their loss releases CO2 and adds to the enhanced greenhouse effect.
**Water cycle**: interception, transpiration and infiltration are high in forests and fall after clearance.
**Rivers**: removing trees increases surface runoff, raising flood risk and silting rivers.
**Sustainable development**: management aims to meet present needs without harming future generations.
**Economic development**: countries such as Brazil develop by using rainforest resources.
**Case study link**: use named Amazon facts when asked to 'use a case study' or 'with reference to a place you have studied'.
**Fieldwork or maps**: you might be asked to read a map or graph showing forest cover.
core.p: Tropical rainforests connect to many other parts of the AQA specification, so you can use these links to build extended answers. The warm, wet climate links to **global atmospheric circulation** and **weather and climate**. The loss of rainforest links to **climate change**, **the water cycle**, **ecosystems and biodiversity** and **sustainable development** (including ecotourism and debt reduction). For the same reason, knowledge of rainforest structure and nutrient cycling is also needed for questions on deforestation, soil erosion and management.

bullets: **Judgement**: the rainforest is fragile because nutrients are mainly stored in the biomass, not in the soil.
**Resilience**: gaps regrow quickly if small, but large-scale clearance is much harder to reverse.
**Competition** drives the many adaptations (reaching light, avoiding predators).
**Specialisation** leads to high biodiversity but makes species vulnerable to habitat change.
Compare with **UK woodland**: lower diversity, seasonal leaf fall, deeper soils.
A 9 mark answer needs **named detail**, **linked explanation** and a **conclusion**.
Avoid generic phrases ('loads of animals'): use precise terminology.
core.h: Higher tier style extension: evaluating and explaining linkages
core.p: For longer answers (6 and 9 marks) you need to go beyond describing: **explain chains of cause and effect**, link several parts of the ecosystem and make a judgement. A good chain might begin with the climate: constant warmth and rain give a long growing season, which produces dense vegetation, which creates layers, which creates many habitats and therefore high biodiversity. Another chain: heavy rain leads to leaching, which would leave soils infertile, but rapid nutrient cycling and shallow roots keep nutrients in the biomass. Practise writing such chains with 'because', 'therefore' and 'this means'.

exam: **Describe** (1 mark per point): give distinct facts with data, e.g. 'temperature is between 26 and 28 °C all year'. Do not explain.
**Explain** (2 to 4 marks): make a point, develop it with 'because' and link it to the cause; each linked step earns a mark.
**Adaptations**: always state the **feature** and its **purpose** (e.g. 'drip tips so rain runs off, reducing fungal growth') for 2 marks.
**Nutrient cycle**: name the three stores, say which is biggest and give a reason (fast decomposition, rapid uptake, leaching).
**Climate graph 2 mark**: one mark for temperature pattern with data, one for rainfall pattern with data.
**Why near the equator? (3 marks)**: high sun angle, intense heating, air rises, condenses, heavy rain.
**4 mark explain interdependence**: pick two or three links, e.g. plants-animals, climate-plants, decomposers-soil, and explain each.
**6 mark**: use a clear structure (introduction, linked points with named examples, conclusion) and relevant terminology.
**Graph tips**: quote units, read the scale accurately, use highest and lowest values, show subtraction for range.
**Use named examples**: toucan, sloth, kapok, bromeliad, poison dart frog; they show detailed knowledge.
**Time**: roughly one mark a minute; do not write long answers to 1 or 2 mark questions.

mistakes.r: The soil is **thin and infertile**; nutrients are held in the **biomass**, not the soil, and are leached by heavy rain.
mistakes.w: Rainforests have fertile soil because the plants grow so well.

mistakes.r: Drip tips help water **run off** quickly so the leaf does not stay wet and grow fungus or be damaged.
mistakes.w: Drip tips help the plant take in water.

mistakes.r: They **support tall trees** in shallow soil and spread out to gather nutrients near the surface.
mistakes.w: Buttress roots take in water from deep underground.

mistakes.r: It is hot and wet because of its **latitude near the equator**: high sun angle, intense heating, rising air and convectional rain.
mistakes.w: The rainforest is hot and wet because it is near the sea.

mistakes.r: They simply **use the tree for support** and take water and nutrients from rain and air.
mistakes.w: Epiphytes are parasites that take food from the tree.

mistakes.r: Decomposition is **very fast** because it is hot and wet, so litter is a small store.
mistakes.w: Decomposition is slow because of the large amount of vegetation.

mistakes.r: Many species share the forest through **niches in different layers**, but competition still exists and drives adaptation.
mistakes.w: Rainforest animals are all in the canopy so there is no competition.

mistakes.r: Rainforests release oxygen but also use much of it; the key global role is as a **carbon store** and in the **water cycle**.
mistakes.w: The rainforest produces most of the world's oxygen.

summary: The specification asks you to describe where tropical rainforests are found, their hot wet equatorial climate, their layered structure, fast nutrient cycle and thin soils, and to explain how plants and animals are adapted and how climate, soil, water, plants, animals and people are interdependent. It matters because it underpins every later question on deforestation and sustainable management, and it is tested with data, diagrams and 4, 6 or 9 mark answers.

terms.d: A forest biome found close to the equator with a hot, wet climate all year, very high biodiversity and several vertical layers.
The variety of plant and animal life in a particular habitat or on Earth as a whole.
The tallest trees that stick out above the canopy and receive full sunlight and wind.
The dense, continuous layer of leaves and branches that forms a roof, absorbing most light and rain and supporting most animal life.
The layer beneath the canopy of young trees and shrubs growing in deep shade.
Large, wide roots that spread out from the base of tall trees to support them in thin soil.
A pointed tip on a leaf that allows heavy rain to run off quickly.
A plant that grows on another plant (usually a tree branch) and takes water and nutrients from the air and rain, not from the soil.
A woody climbing plant that uses trees for support to reach the light.
The movement of nutrients between the biomass, litter and soil stores of an ecosystem.
The total mass of living organisms (plants and animals) in an area; in a rainforest it is the main store of nutrients.
Dead plant material such as fallen leaves that lies on the soil surface and is broken down by decomposers.
The washing of soluble nutrients out of the soil by water draining through it.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants to the atmosphere.
The way in which living things and the physical environment depend on each other within an ecosystem.
An organism, such as a fungus or bacterium, that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil.
Rain caused when the ground is heated, air rises, cools and condenses to form clouds and heavy showers.

worked.ans: The warm, wet climate gives constant growth so trees compete for light and grow tall in layers. The dense **canopy** absorbs most sunlight, so plants in the understorey have large leaves to catch scarce light. Leaves have **drip tips** so heavy rainfall runs off quickly, preventing fungal growth. Tall trees have **buttress roots** to give support in the shallow, nutrient-poor soil. (4 marks)
worked.q: Explain how the structure of tropical rainforest vegetation is adapted to the climate. (4 marks)
steps: Identify the climate features: hot, wet, constant sunlight and heavy rain.
Link to layers: canopy intercepts light, so lower layers are shaded.
Link to leaf features: drip tips, waxy leaves.
Link to roots: buttress roots because of thin soil.

worked.ans: Most nutrients are stored in the **biomass**; the **litter** store is small and the **soil** store is smallest. Leaves fall to form litter, which decomposes quickly in the hot, wet conditions, passing nutrients to the soil. Roots take them up almost immediately, returning them to the biomass. Heavy rain leaches nutrients out of the soil and what remains is absorbed quickly, so the soil contains few nutrients and is infertile even though vegetation is lush. If the trees are removed, the biomass store is lost and nutrients are quickly washed away. (6 marks)
worked.q: Describe the nutrient cycle in a tropical rainforest and explain why the soil is infertile. (6 marks)
steps: Name the stores and relative size: biomass, litter, soil.
Describe the flows: litter fall, decomposition, uptake.
Explain why: fast decomposition, rapid uptake, leaching by heavy rain.
Conclude: nutrients are in the biomass so soil is infertile.

worked.ans: Range = 27 - 25 = **2 °C**. This shows temperatures are almost constant all year, typical of a location near the equator with no true seasons. (2 marks)
worked.q: A climate station shows temperatures of 27 °C in the warmest month and 25 °C in the coolest. Calculate the annual temperature range and say what it shows. (2 marks)
